# Introduction {#intro}

The supplementary material to the  *Polygala lewtonii* dataset from Archbold Biological Station.

The GIS and Data Management program at [Archbold Biological Station](https://www.archbold-station.org/gis-and-data-mgmt/) maintains a comprehensive collection of ecological and environmental data gathered through various research initiatives and ongoing long-term monitoring projects. One key platform for accessing this data is the Archbold Biological Station' [Ecological Data Inventory (EDI)](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/home.jsp), which hosts extensive datasets related to biodiversity, land cover, climate, and ecological patterns.

For our model, we utilized 16 years of demographic data on short-lived herb endemic to fire-maintained Florida sandhills - [*Polygala lewtonii*](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=edi.318.1) using an Integrated Population Model (IPM). This dataset has previously been used in the work of [Weekley and Menges, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1071/BT11271).

# Data {#data}
This [dataset](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/metadataviewer?packageid=edi.318.1) documents the long-term demographic monitoring of 5,060 individually marked *Polygala lewtonii* (Lewton’s milkwort) plants at the Lake Wales Ridge National Wildlife Refuge, Carter Creek, in south-central Florida. From December 2001 to December 2017—and continuing beyond—data were collected quarterly from 220 permanent 25 cm-radius circular plots across six management units in yellow sandhill habitat.

Each plant was marked with a uniquely coded plastic toothpick and flag, and its spatial position within the plot was recorded by angle and distance from the center. Survival and recruitment were recorded four times per year (March, June, September, December), while detailed measurements of size (height, crown diameter, number of stems) and reproductive effort (flowering stem count) were collected each March. Due to the amphicarphic nature of P. lewtonii, only aboveground (chasmogamous) flower data were recorded.

The site experienced four prescribed fires (2001, 2007, 2009, 2015). Post-fire observations included plant-level fire exposure (e.g., singed, scorched, consumed) and percent area burned per plot (except for the 2001 fire). The dataset captures both mortality and recruitment following fire, contributing to an understanding of population responses to disturbance. Importantly, the species does not exhibit dormancy, and plants marked as dead were rarely observed alive in subsequent censuses.

## Tails from meta

*"Plants were censused during their peak of reproduction annually in July and August"*

*"In 220 permanent 25 cm radius circular plots, plants were marked with plastic toothpick"*

*"Data collection occurred quarterly with survival and recruitment recorded in March, June, September and December and more detailed measures of size and fecundity taken in March"*

*"This species is amphicarphic with both showy-open flowers produced in spring (chasmogamy) and closed, self-pollinating flowers both above- and belowground produced in late summer (cleistogamy). Therefore, our fecundity data are based only on chasmogamy."*

*"This dataset also captures post-fire mortality and recruitment events following four prescribed burns."*

*"Plants that had died were given a 'dead' code (0) indicating first time dead but toothpicks and marking flags remained in the field. At the next census, if the plant was still dead, it was given a 'previously dead' code (9) and the toothpick and marking flag were removed from the field."*

*"Plant dormancy does not occur in this species and very few individuals marked as dead were alive in the subsequent census."*

*"In March, we took additional size measures"*

*"four prescribed burns during the 2001-2017 study, although not all plots were affected"*

*"status of the plant as unburned, singed (some green), scorched (no green but brown leaves remained), or consumed (little to no plant material remained)."*

*"P. lewtonii plants are usually killed by fire and seedlings recruit post-fire from a soil seedbank (B. Pace-Aldana, pers. comm.; C. W. Weekley, unpubl. data)."*

*"A separate field experiment demonstrated that buried seeds may retain viability for at least 2 years (C. W. Weekley and E. S. Menges, unpubl. data), indicating that P. lewtonii is capable of accumulating a persistent (sensuThompson and Grime 1979) soil seedbank. The sudden appearance of large cohorts of seedling recruits suggests that the persistent seedbanks of P. lewtonii are ecologically relevant."*

*"In the March 2002 census, burned quadrats out-recruited unburned quadrats 3.7–1 (184.0% v. 49.2%; c2 = 48.880, d.f. = 1, P < 0.001). Over the 2 censuses, burned quadrats had proportional recruitment of between 75.8% and 79.0% of seedlings recruited into burned quadrats with no surviving reproductive adults, indicating that most recruitment was from the preburn seedbank rather than from newly produced seeds."*

## Data exploration

From the [data portal](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=edi.318.1) we get two datasets. 
The first data set contains information about burn status across various quadrants over time. It includes columns for the date, unit number, quadrant identifier, burn status (likely indicating whether a burn event occurred), and the percentage of the area burned. The data spans different dates and quadrants, showing no burn events (burn_status = 0) and mostly zero or NA values for percentage burned, indicating areas that were unburned or had no available data on burning.

The second dataset consists of 196,099 records documenting the life histories of Polygala lewtonii individuals monitored quarterly from 2001 to 2017 across 220 fixed circular plots. Each plant was uniquely located within a plot using a combination of its spatial position (plot unit, quadrat, angle, and distance from plot center), and observed repeatedly through time. For each census, field staff recorded whether the plant was alive, newly dead, or previously dead (plant status), its developmental stage (seedling, juvenile, or adult), structural size (plant height, crown spread, number of stems), and reproductive output (number of flowering stems). Additionally, some plants were flagged as post-fire recruits if they appeared following one of four prescribed burns conducted during the study period.

Initial exploration revealed inconsistencies in plant identification across time. Plant IDs were sometimes reused, with different individuals appearing under the same identifier in different years, occasionally with different spatial coordinates. To resolve this, we redefined plant identity to include both its original tag and its spatial position within the plot, allowing us to track unique individuals throughout the study.

We also identified duplicated entries for the same plant and census period, some with conflicting information about size or status. These duplicates were reviewed and filtered out when necessary. A small number of records had a status code indicating the plant could not be relocated; these were removed due to their ambiguity. Another subset of plants entered the dataset with an undefined status code not described in the field protocol; based on their behavior in subsequent years, we reclassified these as living individuals rather than new recruits.

Several individuals marked as new recruits were never measured for size and died within the same census interval. These contributed no usable demographic information and were excluded to avoid inflating recruitment or mortality rates. For the remaining plants, we reconstructed continuous life histories by ordering observations over time and linking size measurements across consecutive censuses to estimate individual growth trajectories. We calculated derived variables such as above-ground volume (from crown diameter and height) and next-step size values to enable later demographic modeling.

Fire exposure was inconsistently recorded, but we inferred post-fire recruitment by marking individuals that appeared shortly after known burn events. When fire status was missing within a year, we carried forward the highest fire exposure level reported for any individual within that group.

The final processed dataset contains consistently tracked individuals with complete life histories, including identity, spatial location, observation date, survival status, plant developmental stage, structural size, reproductive effort, and fire exposure history. This curated dataset forms a reliable basis for examining how individual-level traits and disturbance history influence population-level dynamics over space and time.



```{r data mean updated}
df <- df_og %>% 
  separate(col = date, into = c('year', 'month'), sep = '-') %>% 
  mutate(id = paste0(unit, '_', quad, '_', id, '_', angle, '-', dist)) %>% 
  arrange(unit, id, year, month) %>% #view()
  # Month of death
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(death = paste0(year, "_", month)[which(survival == 0)[1]]) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Code 2 survival: individual not found, 5 in total. REMOVE
  filter(!id %in% (df_og %>% 
                     mutate(id = paste0(unit, '_', quad, '_', id, '_', angle, '-', dist)) %>%
                     filter(survival == 2) %>% 
                     pull(id) %>% 
                     unique())) %>% #view()
# Fire: For now we will just drag the maximum value of each year with us
  dplyr::select(!c(angle, dist)) %>% #view()
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  mutate(postburn_plant = if_else(all(is.na(postburn_plant)), NA_real_,
                                  max(postburn_plant, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  filter(survival < 9) %>% 
  # Recruits: 5 indicates that the plant was detected for the first time. 
  #  however, there are plants that were detected in a month without size measurement
  #  many of them are present in the next year too.. for now I will count them as recruits too
  #  actually I can give them a 2 - I like it, easy to change later too..
  # Furthermore, 1_609_101_100-19 is an example of how it is not considered a recruit in the original data set
  #  if the plant was there already in the fist year of the sampling campaign (i.e. 2001)
  #  We also don't know if it was or wasn't a recruit and thus it gets an NA
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit = if_else(
      (lag(survival) == 5 & is.na(lag(stage))), 2, 0, missing = 0)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(survival == 5, 1, recruit)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(as.numeric(year) == 2001, NA_real_, recruit)) %>% 
  mutate(recruit = if_else(stage == 1, 1, recruit)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Survival: 
  #  Since there is no dormancy I can remove everything that does not have a size 
  filter(!is.na(stage)) %>% #view()
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    survival = if_else(row_number() == n(), 0, survival)) %>%
  ungroup() %>% #view()
  # Include the NEW ADDITIONS (survival == 3)
  mutate(survival = if_else(survival == 3, 1, survival),
         survival = if_else(survival == 5, 1, survival)) %>% 
  # Growth:
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(size_t1   = lead(height),
         c_dim_t1  = lead(crown_diameter),
         stems_t1  = lead(stems),
         volume_t0 = ((crown_diameter / 2) ^ 2) * pi * height,
         volume_t1 = lead(volume_t0)) %>%
  ungroup()%>% 
  rename(survives = survival,
         size_t0  = height,
         site     = unit) %>% 
  mutate(logsize_t0   = log(size_t0),
         logsize_t1   = log(size_t1),    
         logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,     
         logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3,
         logvol_t0    = log(volume_t0),
         logvol_t1    = log(volume_t1),
         logvol_t0_2  = logvol_t0^2,
         logvol_t0_3  = logvol_t0^3,
         year         = as.numeric(year),
         stage        = as.factor( stage),
         recruits     = if_else(recruit > 0, 1, recruit),
         flower       = if_else(stage == 3, 1, 0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(site, quad, cohort, id, year, 
         stage, survives, size_t0, flower, flowering_stems, recruits, recruit, 
         size_t1, logsize_t1, logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3,
         crown_diameter, stems, postburn_plant,
         volume_t0, volume_t1, logvol_t0, logvol_t1, logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3)

```

# Investigations {#investigation}


```{r Packages}
library(MASS)
```

## Seedbank
There is no information on seed banks in the meta data, nor in the original data.

The published literature and associated unpublished data strongly suggest that Polygala lewtonii relies on a persistent soil seedbank for post-fire recruitment. While the dataset itself contains no direct information on seed banks, several observations and experimental results provide compelling indirect evidence for their ecological importance.

Field observations indicate that most post-fire recruits emerged in quadrats where no surviving reproductive adults were present, implying that recruitment originated from seeds deposited in earlier years. Specifically, the study notes that:

*'For these 2 cohorts, between 75.8% and 79.0% of seedlings recruited into burned quadrats with no surviving reproductive adults, indicating that most recruitment was from the preburn seedbank rather than from newly produced seeds.'*

The timing of recruitment relative to fire and flowering supports this conclusion:

*'Recruits in the first 2 post-burn cohorts (December 2001 and March 2002) came from the seedbank, rather than from seeds shed by surviving adults, which did not produce chasmogamous flowers between the August 2001 burn and the December 2001 and March 2002 censuses.'*

Supporting this field evidence, a separate experiment demonstrated long-term seed viability:


*'A separate field experiment demonstrated that buried seeds may retain viability for at least 2 years (C. W. Weekley and E. S. Menges, unpubl. data), indicating that P. lewtonii is capable of accumulating a persistent (sensu Thompson and Grime 1979) soil seedbank.'*

The study also suggests that fire enhances the reproductive success of recruits, reinforcing the seedbank’s role in population dynamics:

*'The combined effects of higher seedling recruitment, higher survival to reproduction and earlier flowering indicate that P. lewtonii plants recruiting into burned microsites make a greater contribution to the seedbank, and thus to the long-term viability of the population, than do recruits in unburned microsites.'*

While smoke-stimulated germination has been demonstrated in the lab, field evidence is limited:
However in their publication they do not specify any germination rates [(Lindon and Menges, 2008)](https://www.jstor.org/stable/20433949).

*'In a laboratory experiment, Lindon and Menges (2008) showed that short-term exposure to smoke promoted ex situ germination in P. lewtonii, but this result was not supported by a field experiment (C.W. Weekley, unpubl. data).'*

Overall, although the dataset itself does not directly record seedbank dynamics, the documented timing of recruitment, absence of flowering adults, and experimental findings together indicate that P. lewtonii maintains a persistent and ecologically meaningful soil seedbank that plays a key role in its post-fire recovery and long-term persistence.


## Fire

The site experienced four prescribed fires (2001, 2007, 2009, 2015). Post-fire observations included plant-level fire exposure (e.g., singed, scorched, consumed) and percent area burned per plot (except for the 2001 fire). The dataset captures both mortality and recruitment following fire, contributing to an understanding of population responses to disturbance. Importantly, the species does not exhibit dormancy, and plants marked as dead were rarely observed alive in subsequent censuses.

*'This dataset also captures post-fire mortality and recruitment events following four prescribed burns.'*
*'[...] four prescribed burns during the 2001-2017 study, although not all plots were affected'*
*'P. lewtonii plants are usually killed by fire and seedlings recruit post-fire from a soil seedbank (B. Pace-Aldana, pers. comm.; C. W. Weekley, unpubl. data).'*

### The extent of fire
To assess whether visual signs of fire damage on individual plants persist beyond the year of fire, we examined the variable postburn_plant, which records damage severity following prescribed burns. Specifically, we tested whether plants showing fire damage in one year continued to exhibit signs of fire in the subsequent year. Despite repeated prescribed burns in 2001, 2007, 2009, and 2015, our analysis found no evidence that fire damage carries over across years at the individual level. That is, plants recorded as damaged in one year were not marked as damaged again in the following year. This suggests that visible fire effects are either short-lived or not consistently recorded beyond the fire year.
```{r}
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0, TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
  arrange(id, year) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(
    fire_t = fire,
    fire_t1 = lead(fire),       
    year_t1 = lead(year)) %>%
  filter(year_t1 == year + 1) %>% 
  ungroup()

```
To quantify fire severity across space and time, we calculated the proportion of individuals with visible signs of fire damage (postburn_plant > 0) in each plot-year. Only plot-years with at least one scorched individual were included. This metric reflects within-plot fire intensity as experienced by the plant population.
```{r}
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = postburn_plant > 0) %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_fire = sum(fire),
    severity = n_fire / n_total,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_fire > 0)

```
What is up with site 3 quad 539 year 2009
```{r}
df_3_539_2009 <- df %>% 
  filter(site == 3 & quad == 539 & year == 2009)

# Bar plot: Stage by recruits
fig_stage <- ggplot() +
  geom_bar(data = df_3_539_2009, 
           aes(x = stage, 
               fill = as.factor(recruits), 
               color = as.factor(survives)), 
           linewidth = 1) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('0' = '#1b7837', '1' = '#74add1')) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c('0' = '#FFD700', '1' = '#7E57C2')) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(fill = 'Recruit',
       color = 'Survives',
       title = 'Suspect stage, recruitment & survival')

# Histogram: logvol_t0 by recruitment
fig_hist <- ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(data = df_3_539_2009, binwidth = 0.4, 
                 aes(x = logvol_t0, fill = as.factor(recruits))) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('0' = '#1b7837', '1' = '#74add1')) + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(fill = 'Recruit',
       title = 'Suspect size by recruitment status')

# Flat jitter plot for overlap
fig_jitter <- ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = df %>% filter(recruits == 1),
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = 0), 
              height = 0.05, color = '#1ABC9C', alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_3_539_2009 %>% filter(logvol_t0 < 0),
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = 0), 
              height = 0.05, width = 0.1, color = '#8E44AD', alpha = 1, size = 2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "logvol_t0", y = "",
       title = "Suepects against recruit size")

# Matching median logvol_t0
fig_median <- df %>% 
  filter(logvol_t0 == (df_3_539_2009 %>%
                         filter(logvol_t0 < 0) %>%
                         summarise(median(logvol_t0)) %>% pull())) %>% 
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(x = as.factor(recruits))) +
  labs(x = 'Recruit', y = 'Count',
       title = 'Missed recurits potential') +
  theme_bw()

# Combine all plots
(fig_stage | fig_hist) / (fig_jitter | fig_median)

```


To better understand the temporal patterns of fire effects on individual plants, we summarized the presence of fire damage signs (postburn_plant > 0) across months and years. By grouping observations by year and month, we quantified both the number and proportion of individuals exhibiting scorch damage. 
```{r}
df_og %>%
  separate(col = date, into = c("year", "month"), sep = "-") %>%
  filter(!is.na(postburn_plant)) %>%
  mutate(fire = postburn_plant > 0) %>%
  group_by(year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    n_total = n(),
    n_fire = sum(fire),
    pct_fire = round(100 * n_fire / n_total, 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(year, month)
```

### Fire on Survival
```{r su_f data}
df_su <- df %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F)) %>% 
  filter(size_t0 != 0) %>%
  mutate(fire_label = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire')) %>%
  dplyr::select(id, year, survives,
         logvol_t0, logvol_t1, logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3,
         fire, fire_label)

# Create binned summary using group_split()
df_su_binned <- df_su %>%
  group_split(fire_label) %>%
  purrr::map_df(~ plot_binned_prop(.x, 10, logvol_t0, survives) %>%
                  mutate(fire_label = unique(.x$fire_label)))

fig_su_overall <- ggplot(df_su_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_su, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
              position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.3), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9), limits = c(0, 1.01)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 8),
    title = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.position = 'top') +
  labs(
    title = 'Survival',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x = expression('Volume (log)'[t0]),
    y = 'Survival Probability\nfrom time t0 to t1 ',
    color = 'At time t0')

fig_su_overall
```
```{r su_f model}
# Logistic regression
mod_su_0 <- glm(survives ~ fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial') 
# Logistic regression
mod_su_1 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial') 
# Quadratic logistic model
mod_su_2 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial')  
# Cubic logistic model
mod_su_3 <- glm(survives ~ logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3 + fire,
                data = df_su, family = 'binomial')  


# Compare models using AIC
mods_su      <- list(mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)
mods_su_dAIC <- AICtab(mods_su, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

# Get the sorted indices of dAIC values
mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAIC)

# Establish the index of model complexity
if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index       <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1 
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su +1
  v_mod_su_index       <- v_mod_set_su}

mod_su_bestfit <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]
mod_su_ranef   <- coef(mod_su_bestfit)

# Create prediction data frames for fire = 0 and fire = 1
df_su_pred <- data.frame(
  logvol_t0 = rep(seq(min(na.omit(df_su$logvol_t0)), 
                      max(na.omit(df_su$logvol_t0)), length.out = 100), 2),
  fire = rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = 100)) %>% 
  mutate(logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
         fire_label = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire')) %>% 
  mutate(survives = predict(mod_su_bestfit, newdata = ., type = 'response'))

# Binned observed data for both fire levels
df_su_binned <- bind_rows(
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_su, fire == 0), 10, logvol_t0, survives) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'No fire'),
  plot_binned_prop(filter(df_su, fire == 1), 10, logvol_t0, survives) %>%
    mutate(fire_label = 'Fire'))

# Plot 1: Raw data + prediction lines
fig_su_line_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_jitter(data = df_su, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
              alpha = 0.25, width = 0.08, height = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = df_su_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +  
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Volume at time t0 (log)', y = 'Survival to time t1') +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')

# Plot 2: Binned proportions + prediction lines
fig_su_bin_combined <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = df_su_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_errorbar(data = df_su_binned, aes(x = logvol_t0, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, color = fire_label),
                width = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = df_su_pred, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = survives, color = fire_label),
            linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1) +
  labs(title = NULL, x = 'Volume at time t0 (log)', y = 'Survival to time t1', 
       color = 'At time t0') +
  theme(legend.position = 'top')

# Combine the two plots
fig_su_all <- fig_su_line_combined + fig_su_bin_combined +
  plot_annotation(
    title = 'Survival',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = 'bold'),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, face = 'italic')))

fig_su_all
```

### Fire on Fecundity
```{r fe_f}
df_fe <- df %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F),
         fire_label = if_else(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire')) %>% 
  filter(flower == 1, !is.na(logvol_t0)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(flowering_stems, fire, fire_label, 
                logvol_t0, logvol_t0_2, logvol_t0_3)


```


```{r fe_model}
mod_fe_0 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_1 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_2 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2, data = df_fe)
mod_fe_3 <- glm.nb(flowering_stems ~ fire + logvol_t0 + logvol_t0_2 + logvol_t0_3, data = df_fe)

mods_fe      <- list(mod_fe_0, mod_fe_1, mod_fe_2, mod_fe_3)
mods_fe_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_fe, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC
mods_fe_i_sort <- order(mods_fe_dAIC)

if (length(v_mod_set_fe) == 0) {
  mod_fe_i_best <- mods_fe_i_sort[1]
  v_mod_fe_i    <- mod_fe_i_best - 1 
} else {
  mod_fe_i_best <- v_mod_set_fe +1
  v_mod_fe_i    <- v_mod_set_fe
  }

mod_fe_best  <- mods_fe[[mod_fe_i_best]]
mod_fe_ranef <- coef(mod_fe_best)

df_fe_preddata <- tibble(
  logvol_t0 = rep(seq(min(df_fe$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
                  max(df_fe$logvol_t0, na.rm = TRUE),
                  length.out = 100), 2),
  fire       = rep(c(F, T), each = 100)) %>%
  mutate(logvol_t0_2 = logvol_t0^2,
         logvol_t0_3 = logvol_t0^3,
         fire_label  = ifelse(fire == 1, 'Fire', 'No fire'))

mod_fe_pred <- predict(mod_fe_best, newdata = df_fe_preddata, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)

df_fe_preddata <- df_fe_preddata %>%
  mutate(
    fit_link = mod_fe_pred$fit,
    se_link  = mod_fe_pred$se.fit,
    fit_link_lower = fit_link - 1.96 * se_link,
    fit_link_upper = fit_link + 1.96 * se_link,
    predicted_stems = exp(fit_link),
    predicted_stems_lower = exp(fit_link_lower),
    predicted_stems_upper = exp(fit_link_upper))

fig_fe <- ggplot(df_fe, aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label)) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fe %>% filter(fire == F), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label),
              width = 0.1, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_jitter(data = df_fe %>% filter(fire == T), 
              aes(x = logvol_t0, y = flowering_stems, color = fire_label),
              width = 0.1, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = df_fe_preddata, 
            aes(x = logvol_t0, y = predicted_stems, color = fire_label), size = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = df_fe_preddata,
    aes(x = logvol_t0, ymin = predicted_stems_lower, ymax = predicted_stems_upper, fill = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.1, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No fire' = 'black', 'Fire' = 'red')) +
  labs(
    title    = 'Fecundity',
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x        = 'Volume t0 (log)',
    y        = 'Number of Flowering Stems\nin time t0',
    color    = 'At time t0',
    fill     = 'At time t0') +
  theme_bw()
fig_fe

```


### Fire on Recruitment transition
This analysis examines how the total number of flowering stems in year t influences recruitment in year t+1, and whether this relationship is affected by fire in the previous year.

```{r}
df_fs2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F)) %>%
  summarise(
    total_stocks = sum(flowering_stems, na.rm = TRUE),
    fire = any(fire == T),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  full_join(df %>%
               group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
               summarise(
                 recruit_count_t1 = sum(recruits, na.rm = TRUE),
                 .groups = 'drop') %>%
               mutate(year = year - 1), 
             by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  mutate(fire_label = ifelse(fire, "Fire", "No Fire"))
  
mod_fs2r_01 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ fire, data = df_fs2r)
mod_fs2r_02 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks + fire, data = df_fs2r)
mod_fs2r_11 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks * fire, data = df_fs2r)

mods_fs2r      <- list(mod_fs2r_01,  mod_fs2r_02, mod_fs2r_11)
mods_fs2r_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_fs2r, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

# Plot: Effect of fire only (mod_fs2r_01)
df_fs2r_newdata <- data.frame(fire = c(FALSE, TRUE))
df_fs2r_newdata$fit <- predict(mod_fs2r_01, newdata = df_fs2r_newdata, type = 'response')
pred_link <- predict(mod_fs2r_01, newdata = df_fs2r_newdata, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)
df_fs2r_newdata$lower <- exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit)
df_fs2r_newdata$upper <- exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit)
df_fs2r_newdata$fire <- factor(df_fs2r_newdata$fire, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c('No Fire', 'Fire'))

ggplot(df_fs2r_newdata, aes(x = fire, y = fit, fill = fire)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = 'gray30') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, color = 'gray30') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) + 
  labs(
    x = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire on Recruitment') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')


# Plot: Effect of total_stocks and fire interaction (mod_fs2r_11)
df_fs2r_predgrid <- df_fs2r %>%
  filter(total_stocks < 100) %>%
  group_by(fire) %>%
  summarise(
    min_ts = min(total_stocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_ts = max(total_stocks, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_stocks_seq = list(seq(min_ts, max_ts, length.out = 100))) %>%
  unnest(total_stocks_seq) %>%
  rename(total_stocks = total_stocks_seq)

# Predict
pred_link <- predict(mod_fs2r_11, newdata = df_fs2r_predgrid, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)

df_fs2r_predgrid <- df_fs2r_predgrid %>%
  mutate(
    fit   = exp(pred_link$fit),
    lower = exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    upper = exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    fire_label = ifelse(fire, 'Fire', 'No Fire'))

# Plot
ggplot(df_fs2r_predgrid, aes(x = total_stocks, y = fit, color = fire_label, fill = fire_label)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_fs2r %>% filter(total_stocks < 100 & fire_label == 'No Fire'),
    aes(x = total_stocks, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.1, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_fs2r %>% filter(total_stocks < 100 & fire_label == 'Fire'),
    aes(x = total_stocks, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  labs(
    x = 'Total Flowering Stems (t)',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire and Flowering Stems on Recruitment',
    color = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    fill  = 'Fire in Previous Year') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)
```
Here, we focus on whether the number of mature, reproductive individuals (stage 3 plants) in a plot during year t predicts recruitment in the following year and Fire.
```{r}
df_ir2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
  filter(stage == 3) %>% 
  summarise(
    fire = any(fire == TRUE),
    nr_repro_indiv = n(),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  full_join(
    df %>%
      group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
      summarise(
        recruit_count_t1 = sum(recruits, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = 'drop') %>%
      mutate(year = year - 1), 
    by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  mutate(
    fire_label = ifelse(fire, 'Fire', 'No Fire'))

mod_ir2r_01 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ fire, data = df_ir2r)
mod_ir2r_02 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv + fire, data = df_ir2r)
mod_ir2r_11 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv * fire, data = df_ir2r)

mods_ir2r      <- list(mod_ir2r_01,  mod_ir2r_02, mod_ir2r_11)
mods_ir2r_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_ir2r, weights = TRUE, sort = FALSE)$dAIC

df_ir2r_newdata <- data.frame(fire = c(FALSE, TRUE))
pred_link <- predict(mod_ir2r_01, newdata = df_ir2r_newdata, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)
df_ir2r_newdata <- df_ir2r_newdata %>%
  mutate(
    fit   = exp(pred_link$fit),
    lower = exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    upper = exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    fire  = factor(fire, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c('No Fire', 'Fire')))

ggplot(df_ir2r_newdata, aes(x = fire, y = fit, fill = fire)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, color = 'gray30') +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2, color = 'gray30') +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  labs(
    x = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire on Recruitment') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = 'none')


df_ir2r_predgrid <- df_ir2r %>%
  filter(nr_repro_indiv < 100) %>%
  group_by(fire) %>%
  summarise(
    min_nr = min(nr_repro_indiv, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_nr = max(nr_repro_indiv, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(nr_seq = list(seq(min_nr, max_nr, length.out = 100))) %>%
  unnest(nr_seq) %>%
  rename(nr_repro_indiv = nr_seq) %>%
  mutate(fire = as.logical(fire))  

pred_link <- predict(mod_ir2r_11, newdata = df_ir2r_predgrid, type = 'link', se.fit = TRUE)
df_ir2r_predgrid <- df_ir2r_predgrid %>%
  mutate(
    fit   = exp(pred_link$fit),
    lower = exp(pred_link$fit - 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    upper = exp(pred_link$fit + 1.96 * pred_link$se.fit),
    fire_label = ifelse(fire, 'Fire', 'No Fire')
  )

ggplot(df_ir2r_predgrid, aes(x = nr_repro_indiv, y = fit, color = fire_label, fill = fire_label)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_ir2r %>% filter(nr_repro_indiv < 100 & fire_label == 'No Fire'),
    aes(x = nr_repro_indiv, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.1, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = df_ir2r %>% filter(nr_repro_indiv < 100 & fire_label == 'Fire'),
    aes(x = nr_repro_indiv, y = recruit_count_t1, color = fire_label),
    alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8, width = 0.3, height = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c('No Fire' = '#1b9e77', 'Fire' = '#d95f02')) +
  labs(
    x = 'Number of Reproductive Individuals (t)',
    y = 'Predicted Recruitment Count (t+1)',
    title = 'Effect of Fire and Reproductive Individuals on Recruitment',
    color = 'Fire in Previous Year',
    fill  = 'Fire in Previous Year') +
  theme_bw(base_size = 14)
```

This broader model includes all observed individuals (regardless of life stage), evaluating the relationship between total reproductive presence and subsequent recruitment.

```{r}
df_2r <- df %>%
  group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_stocks = sum(flowering_stems, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  full_join(df %>%
              group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
              mutate(fire = if_else(
                postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), TRUE, FALSE)) %>%
              filter(stage == 3) %>%
              summarise(
                nr_repro_indiv = n(),
                .groups = 'drop'), 
            by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  full_join(df %>%
              group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
              mutate(fire = if_else(postburn_plant > 0 & !is.na(postburn_plant), T, F)) %>%
              summarise(
                nr_total_indiv = n(),
                fire = any(fire == T),
                .groups = 'drop'), 
            by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>%
  full_join(df %>%
              group_by(site, quad, year) %>%
              summarise(
                recruit_count_t1 = sum(recruits, na.rm = TRUE),
                .groups = 'drop') %>%
              mutate(year = year - 1), 
            by = c('site', 'quad', 'year')) %>% 
  drop_na()

# Models
mod_2r_00 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ fire,                  data = df_2r)
mod_2r_11 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks   + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_12 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ total_stocks   * fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_21 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_22 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_repro_indiv * fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_31 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_total_indiv + fire, data = df_2r)
mod_2r_32 <- glm.nb(recruit_count_t1 ~ nr_total_indiv * fire, data = df_2r)

mods_2r      <- list(
  mod_2r_00, mod_2r_11, mod_2r_12, mod_2r_21, mod_2r_22, mod_2r_31, mod_2r_32)
mods_2r_dAIC <- AICctab(mods_2r, weights = T, sort = F)$dAIC

```

# Updated data {#data_debugged}

This chapter documents the updated *Polygala lewtonii* dataset and the
construction of the revised working data. The new dataset is not simply an
extension of the data described in Chapter \@ref(data). It adds observations
from more recent years, reorganizes the original data structure, and provides
additional information at the individual, quadrat, and site levels.
Consequently, the complete data-processing workflow was reviewed and updated.

The main aim of this chapter is to describe the newly provided files, compare
them with the data used in Chapter \@ref(data), document the decisions made
during data cleaning, and explain how the final working dataset was produced.

## Overview

The updated data were provided as an Excel workbook containing four principal
worksheets: `Demog_longform`, `Demog`, `QuadLevel`, and `SiteHistory`. Each
worksheet is accompanied by separate metadata describing its variables and
coding.

The demographic records now extend through 2025. In addition to the longer
study period, the updated workbook separates repeated demographic
observations, quadrat-level information, and site-level management history
more clearly than the dataset used in Chapter \@ref(data). These structural
changes required us to reassess plant identity, annual transitions,
recruitment, mortality, growth, and disturbance exposure before constructing
the revised working dataset.


```{r 8_setup}
library(dplyr)

file_workbook <- paste0(
  "C:/code/RUPDemo_IPMs/archbold/data/pole/",
  "Pol_lew_CCS_2025_complete.xlsx")

df_workbook_sheets <- tibble(
  sheet = readxl::excel_sheets(file_workbook)) %>%
  mutate(
    type = if_else(
      str_detect(sheet, "metadata$"),
      "Metadata", "Data"),
    dataset = str_remove(sheet, " metadata$")) %>%
  dplyr::select(dataset, type, sheet)

knitr::kable(
  df_workbook_sheets,
  col.names = c("Dataset", "Worksheet type", "Worksheet name"))
```

`Demog_longform` contains the repeated demographic censuses,
whereas `Demog` provides the demographic records in a wider format.
`QuadLevel` contains information recorded at the quadrat level, and
`SiteHistory` documents disturbance and management history at the site level.

```{r data-debugged-dataset-dimensions}
data_sheets <- c(
  "Demog_longform", "Demog", "QuadLevel", "SiteHistory")

df_dataset_dimensions <- map_dfr(data_sheets, function(sheet_i) {
  data_i <- readxl::read_excel(file_workbook, sheet = sheet_i)

  tibble(
    dataset = sheet_i,
    rows = nrow(data_i),
    columns = ncol(data_i))
})

knitr::kable(
  df_dataset_dimensions,
  col.names = c("Dataset", "Rows", "Columns"))
```

```{r data-debugged-read-sheets, include=FALSE}
df_demog_long <- readxl::read_excel(
  file_workbook,
  sheet = "Demog_longform",
  na = c("", "NA")) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

df_demog_wide <- readxl::read_excel(
  file_workbook,
  sheet = "Demog",
  na = c("", "NA")) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

df_quad <- readxl::read_excel(
  file_workbook,
  sheet = "QuadLevel",
  na = c("", "NA")) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

df_site <- readxl::read_excel(
  file_workbook,
  sheet = "SiteHistory",
  col_types = c("numeric", "text", "text", "text")) %>%
  janitor::clean_names() %>%
  mutate(
    date = case_when(
      is.na(date) ~ NA_character_,
      str_detect(date, "^\\d+$") ~ format(
        as.Date(
          as.numeric(date),
          origin = "1899-12-30"),
        "%m/%d/%Y"),
      TRUE ~ date))
```


## Data worksheets


### Demog_longform

`Demog_longform` is the main demographic dataset used in this analysis. It
contains 43,869 observations and 12 variables. Each row represents one
individual plant during one quarterly census. Plants are identified by a
unique individual ID and linked to their quadrat and patch.

Survival was recorded during the quarterly censuses in March, June, September,
and December. Stage, height, maximum crown diameter, stem number, and flowering
stem number were generally recorded during the annual March census. The first
annual census was carried out in April 2001.

Compared with the dataset used in Chapter \@ref(data), the updated long-format
dataset extends the demographic record through 2025 and already contains a
consistent `unique_ID`.

```{r data-debugged-show-demog-long}
df_demog_long %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### Demog

`Demog` contains 7,424 rows and 309 columns. It stores the demographic history
in wide format, with one row per individual and separate columns for each
census date. For example, survival, stage, height, crown diameter, stem number,
and flowering stem number are stored in variables such as `surv0325`,
`stg0325`, and `ht0325`.

The two demographic worksheets therefore contain much of the same underlying
information but organize it differently. `Demog`
retains additional information such as cohort, plant position, comments,
annual-survival variables, and historical post-burn measurements.


### QuadLevel

`QuadLevel` contains one row for each of the 220 permanent quadrats. It includes
the quadrat coordinates, treatment block, patch, monitoring level, recent
plant counts, flowering-stem counts, stem counts, occupancy, and measurements
of the 2022 prescribed burn.

This worksheet is particularly important for understanding the change in
sampling after June 2022. Some quadrats continued under Level 3 individual
demographic monitoring, whereas the remaining quadrats were reduced to Level 2
count-based monitoring. The Level 2 observations are stored in this worksheet
rather than in the individual demographic dataset.


```{r data-debugged-show-quad}
df_quad %>%
  dplyr::select(
    patch, quad, lvl3, n2025, flst0325, stm0325,
    n2024, flst0324, stm0324, n2023,
    postburn_status0322, postburn_pct0322) %>%
  dplyr::slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

### SiteHistory

`SiteHistory` provides a chronological record of major natural disturbances
and management events at the study site. The worksheet includes prescribed
burns in 2001, 2007, 2009, 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2022, several hurricanes in
2004, Hurricane Irma in 2017, and hardwood reduction in 2023.

This is an important addition to the data described in Chapter \@ref(data),
which only included the four prescribed burns up to 2015. Fire is central to
the demography of *P. lewtonii*: established plants are commonly killed by
fire, while large seedling cohorts can recruit from the persistent soil
seedbank after burning. Other disturbances, including hurricanes and hardwood
removal, may also alter survival, recruitment, vegetation cover, and the
availability of open habitat. Disturbance history is therefore treated as a
central part of the demographic data rather than only as background site
information.

Note to the data provider: The date recorded for the 2015 prescribed burn incorrectly gives the year 2025. This is a known typographical error, and the event is treated as a 2015
burn throughout the analysis.

```{r data-debugged-show-site-history}
(df_site) %>% print()
```

## Differences from the previous dataset

The updated dataset differs from the data used in Chapter \@ref(data) in both
its time span and structure. The earlier dataset covered the monitoring period
from 2001 to 2017, whereas the updated demographic records extend through
2025.

```{r data-debugged-differences}
df_data_differences <- tribble(
  ~Aspect, ~`Previous dataset`, ~`Updated dataset`,
  "Study period",
  "2001--2017",
  "2001--2025",
  "Plant identity",
  paste(
    "Identity reconstructed from management unit, quadrat, plant tag,",
    "angle, and distance"),
  "A unique individual identifier is supplied",
  "Demographic structure",
  "Quarterly observations stored in one main table",
  paste(
    "Quarterly long-format data and individual-level wide-format data",
    "are supplied separately"),
  "Spatial information",
  "Stored together with the demographic observations",
  paste(
    "Additional quadrat-level information is supplied in",
    "`QuadLevel`"),
  "Disturbance history",
  "Four prescribed burns through 2015",
  paste(
    "Prescribed burns through 2022 and additional disturbance history",
    "are supplied"),
  "Monitoring design",
  "Individual demographic monitoring across the permanent quadrats",
  paste(
    "Level 3 individual monitoring and Level 2 count monitoring are",
    "distinguished after 2022"))

knitr::kable(df_data_differences)
```

The supplied unique individual identifier is an improvement. In the
previous analysis, plant tags were not always unique through time and plant
identity therefore had to be reconstructed from the tag and its position
within the quadrat. The updated `unique_ID` variable removes this step and is
used as the individual identifier throughout the revised data preparation.

The updated workbook also separates information that was previously combined
within the demographic records. Repeated demographic observations are taken
from `Demog_longform`, while additional individual, quadrat, and disturbance
information can be obtained from the other worksheets. This provides more
information, but also requires the different spatial and temporal levels of
the data to be handled explicitly.

The revised working-data procedure was therefore rebuilt rather than simply
applied to the additional years. In particular, recruitment timing, annual
survival, growth transitions, and disturbance exposure were checked again
against the quarterly census structure.


## Construction of the annual demographic dataset

The demographic data contain quarterly observations, but the IPMs describe
transitions between annual censuses. The annual dataset was therefore created
by retaining records with a recorded stage. Stage, plant size, stem number, and
flowering stem number were normally measured during the March census. The
initial annual census was conducted in April 2001.

Annual census records were identified by the presence of a stage
classification. Unlike filtering by height or crown diameter, this approach
also retains individuals with incomplete size measurements, including
confirmed recruits that could not be assigned a volume.

```{r data-debugged-annual-data}
df_annual <- df_demog_long %>%
  rename(id = unique_id) %>%
  filter(!is.na(stg)) %>%
  arrange(id, year, month)

n_annual_duplicates <- df_annual %>%
  count(id, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  nrow()

df_annual_summary <- df_annual %>%
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    individuals = n_distinct(id),
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    sites = n_distinct(patch),
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE))

knitr::kable(
  df_annual_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Annual records", "Individuals", "Quadrats", "Sites",
    "First year", "Last year"))
```

Each row in the resulting dataset represents one individual at one annual
census. No duplicated individual-year records were found
(`r n_annual_duplicates` cases).

```{r data-debugged-annual-census-timing}
df_census_timing <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    years = n_distinct(year),
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop")

knitr::kable(
  df_census_timing,
  col.names = c(
    "Census month", "First year", "Last year",
    "Number of years", "Annual records"))
```

The April records belong exclusively to the first census in 2001. All
subsequent annual records were collected in March. The annual transition
represented by a row therefore generally begins in March of year \(t\) and
ends in March of year \(t+1\). The first transition begins in April 2001 and
ends in March 2002.


## Recruitment

Recruitment was identified from the quarterly survival code `qsurv == 5`,
which records the first observation of an individual as a seedling. Recruitment
was assigned to the annual census at the end of the corresponding census
interval.

Seedlings recorded during March were assigned to that census year. Seedlings
first recorded from June to December were assigned to the following annual
census. Recruitment in 2001 was left as unknown because the first census
represents the beginning of the study rather than a complete annual
recruitment interval.

```{r data-debugged-recruitment}
df_recruit <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(qsurv == 5) %>%
  transmute(
    id = unique_id,
    recruit_year = case_when(
      year == 2001 & month == 4 ~ 2001,
      month > 3 ~ year + 1,
      TRUE ~ year)) %>%
  distinct(id, recruit_year) %>%
  mutate(recruit_qsurv = 1)

df_annual_recruit <- df_annual %>%
  left_join(
    df_recruit,
    by = c("id", "year" = "recruit_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit = case_when(
      year == 2001 ~ NA_real_,
      recruit_qsurv == 1 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0))

df_recruit_summary <- df_annual_recruit %>%
  summarise(
    confirmed_recruits = sum(recruit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    non_recruits = sum(recruit == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    baseline_unknown = sum(is.na(recruit)))

knitr::kable(
  df_recruit_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Confirmed recruits", "Non-recruits",
    "Unknown baseline records"))
```

The previous preparation combined three criteria: the immediately preceding
quarterly survival code, the current quarterly survival code, and annual stage
1. This could miss seedlings first observed earlier in the annual interval if
later quarterly observations occurred before the annual census.

The revised method searches the complete interval for a confirmed seedling
record and does not depend on the immediately preceding observation. Annual
stage is not used to define recruitment. Individuals recorded as new adults
(`qsurv == 3`) are also not classified as recruits because their seedling
status during that year cannot be confirmed. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}



## Survival and growth transitions

Survival and growth were defined over the interval between consecutive annual
censuses. All recorded deaths (`qsurv == 0`) occurring after the census in year
\(t\) and no later than the census in year \(t+1\) were assigned to that annual
transition.

A recorded death was treated as direct evidence of mortality during the annual
transition. In a small number of cases, an individual was coded as dead during
one quarterly census but was recorded again at a later quarterly census within
the same annual interval. However, the individual was absent from the next
full annual census and did not appear in subsequent annual records. The later
quarterly observation was therefore not interpreted as survival to \(t+1\).

The annual transition containing the death was classified as
`survives = 0`. Any later quarterly size measurement within that interval was
not used as the individual's size at \(t+1\), so the transition was also
excluded from the growth data.

| Census | Observation | Interpretation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| March, year \(t\) | Individual measured during the annual census | Alive at \(t\) |
| June, year \(t\) | Individual coded as dead (`qsurv = 0`) | Death occurred during the transition |
| September, year \(t\) | Individual recorded again during a quarterly census | Does not override the death record |
| March, year \(t+1\) | Individual absent from the annual census | `survives = 0`; no growth transition |

```{r data-debugged-survival-growth}
df_death_interval <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(!is.na(stg)) %>%
  transmute(
    id = unique_id, year,
    census_time = year * 12 + month,
    target_time = (year + 1) * 12 + 3) %>%
  left_join(
    df_demog_long %>%
      filter(qsurv == 0) %>%
      transmute(
        id = unique_id,
        death_time = year * 12 + month),
    by = "id", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarise(
    death_in_interval = any(
      !is.na(death_time) &
        death_time > census_time &
        death_time <= target_time),
    .groups = "drop")

df_transitions <- df_annual_recruit %>%
  left_join(df_death_interval, by = c("id", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    death_in_interval = replace_na(death_in_interval, FALSE)) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  arrange(year, month, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    next_year = lead(year),
    last_observed_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    annual_transition = coalesce(next_year == year + 1, FALSE),
    observed_later = last_observed_year > year,
    valid_growth_transition =
      annual_transition & !death_in_interval,
    survives = case_when(
      death_in_interval ~ 0,
      annual_transition ~ 1,
      observed_later ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  ungroup()

df_transition_summary <- df_transitions %>%
  summarise(
    recorded_deaths = sum(death_in_interval),
    observed_survival = sum(
      annual_transition & !death_in_interval),
    inferred_survival = sum(
      observed_later & !annual_transition &
        !death_in_interval),
    unknown_survival = sum(is.na(survives)),
    growth_transitions = sum(valid_growth_transition))

knitr::kable(
  df_transition_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Recorded deaths",
    "Observed survival",
    "Survival inferred from later observations",
    "Unknown survival",
    "Valid growth transitions"))
```

When an individual was not recorded in year \(t+1\), but was observed again in
a later year, it was considered to have survived the first transition. This
accounts for known gaps in annual sampling. Growth was not reconstructed across
these gaps because no consecutive size measurement was available.

Growth measurements at \(t+1\) were retained only when the individual was
recorded in the following annual census and no death occurred during the
transition.



## Disturbance

Disturbance was assigned at the quadrat level rather than the site level.
Prescribed burns did not affect every quadrat within a site equally. In the
updated data, several site-year combinations contain both disturbed and
undisturbed quadrats. Aggregating disturbance to the site level would therefore
remove observed spatial variation.

The disturbance variable describes whether a quadrat was affected by fire
during an annual transition. A recorded fire effect was coded as 1 and an
explicitly unburned quadrat was coded as 0. A missing classification was
retained as `NA`, because it provides no evidence that the quadrat was
unburned.

### Source of the 2022 fire classification

Fire information through 2020 was obtained from the historical post-burn
variables in `Demog`. The 2022 fire classification was instead obtained from
`QuadLevel`.

The metadata for `postburn_status0322` distinguishes three possible values:
1 for burned, 0 for unburned, and `NA` for a missing plot. However, the workbook
does not establish why a classification is missing. A missing value could
represent a missing field observation, incomplete data entry, or another
unrecorded reason. It is therefore described here simply as having no recorded
classification.

The two worksheets were compared before selecting the source of the 2022
variable.

```{r data-debugged-disturbance-source}
df_dist_2022_demog <- df_demog_wide %>%
  filter(!is.na(quad)) %>%
  group_by(quad) %>%
  summarise(
    dist_2022_demog = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_status0322)),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(
        any(postburn_status0322 == 1, na.rm = TRUE))),
    .groups = "drop")

df_dist_2022 <- df_quad %>%
  transmute(
    quad,
    dist_2022 = as.numeric(postburn_status0322))

df_2022_source_summary <- df_dist_2022 %>%
  left_join(
    df_dist_2022_demog,
    by = "quad") %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n(),
    missing_in_quadlevel = sum(is.na(dist_2022)),
    missing_in_demog = sum(is.na(dist_2022_demog)),
    available_in_quadlevel_but_missing_in_demog = sum(
      !is.na(dist_2022) &
        is.na(dist_2022_demog)),
    conflicting_values = sum(
      !is.na(dist_2022) &
        !is.na(dist_2022_demog) &
        dist_2022 != dist_2022_demog))

knitr::kable(
  df_2022_source_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Quadrats",
    "Missing in QuadLevel",
    "Missing in Demog",
    "Available only in QuadLevel",
    "Conflicting values"))
```

`QuadLevel` contained an explicit 2022 classification for
`r df_2022_source_summary$available_in_quadlevel_but_missing_in_demog`
quadrats that lacked the corresponding information in `Demog`. There were
`r df_2022_source_summary$conflicting_values` conflicts among quadrats with
information in both worksheets. `QuadLevel` was therefore used as the source
of the 2022 fire classification.

Only `r df_2022_source_summary$missing_in_quadlevel` actual quadrat lacked a
recorded 2022 classification. This quadrat was retained as `NA` rather than
being added to the explicitly unburned group.

### Assignment to annual transitions

For the fires through 2020, a positive post-burn category was coded as 1 and a
recorded category of zero was coded as 0. If all relevant measurements were
missing during a known fire event, the classification remained `NA`. The 2022
classification was joined from `QuadLevel`.

```{r data-debugged-disturbance}
df_dist_event <- df_demog_wide %>%
  filter(!is.na(quad)) %>%
  group_by(quad) %>%
  summarise(
    dist_2001 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_status1201)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_status1201 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2007 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct1207)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct1207 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2009 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0609)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0609 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2015 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0615)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0615 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2019 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0319)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0319 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    dist_2020 = if_else(
      all(is.na(postburn_pct0120)), NA_real_,
      as.numeric(any(
        postburn_pct0120 > 0,
        na.rm = TRUE))),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(
    df_dist_2022,
    by = "quad")

df_dist_transition <- bind_rows(
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2001,
      dist_transition = dist_2001),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2007,
      dist_transition = dist_2007),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2009,
      dist_transition = dist_2009),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2015,
      dist_transition = dist_2015),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2018,
      dist_transition = dist_2019),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2019,
      dist_transition = dist_2020),
  df_dist_event %>%
    transmute(
      quad,
      year = 2021,
      dist_transition = dist_2022))

df_transitions_dist <- df_transitions %>%
  left_join(
    df_dist_transition,
    by = c("quad", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    dist_transition = case_when(
      year %in% c(
        2001, 2007, 2009, 2015,
        2018, 2019, 2021) ~
        dist_transition,
      TRUE ~ 0))

n_mixed_site_years <- df_transitions_dist %>%
  filter(!is.na(dist_transition)) %>%
  distinct(
    patch,
    year,
    dist_transition) %>%
  count(patch, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  nrow()

df_disturbance_mapping <- tribble(
  ~`Fire year`, ~`Source`, ~`Source variable`,
  ~`Transition year`,
  2001, "Demog", "postburn_status1201", 2001,
  2007, "Demog", "postburn_pct1207", 2007,
  2009, "Demog", "postburn_pct0609", 2009,
  2015, "Demog", "postburn_pct0615", 2015,
  2019, "Demog", "postburn_pct0319", 2018,
  2020, "Demog", "postburn_pct0120", 2019,
  2022, "QuadLevel", "postburn_status0322", 2021) %>%
  left_join(
    df_transitions_dist %>%
      filter(is.na(dist_transition)) %>%
      count(
        year,
        name = "Missing annual records"),
    by = c("Transition year" = "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    `Missing annual records` = replace_na(
      `Missing annual records`,
      0L))

knitr::kable(df_disturbance_mapping)
```

The fire event was assigned to the annual transition during which it occurred.
The fires in 2001, 2007, 2009, and 2015 occurred after the annual census and
were assigned to transitions beginning in those years. The fires in 2019,
2020, and 2022 were assigned to the transitions ending in those years.

Disturbance differed among quadrats within
`r n_mixed_site_years` site-year combinations, supporting its retention at the
quadrat level. In total,
`r sum(is.na(df_transitions_dist$dist_transition))` annual records have no
recorded fire classification during a known fire transition. The number
associated with each fire is reported in the final column of the table.




## Final working dataset

The cleaned annual records were exported as the working dataset used by the
demographic models. The dataset retains the site, quadrat, individual, and year
identifiers so that observations can be analysed at the appropriate spatial
and temporal levels.

```{r data-debugged-final-working-data}
file_workdata <- file.path(
  dirname(file_workbook),
  "ab_pole_df_workdata_260519.csv")

df_work <- readr::read_csv(
  file_workdata,
  show_col_types = FALSE)

df_work_summary <- df_work %>%
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    individuals = n_distinct(id),
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    sites = n_distinct(site),
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    recruits = sum(recruit == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    deaths = sum(survives == 0, na.rm = TRUE))

knitr::kable(
  df_work_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Records", "Individuals", "Quadrats", "Sites",
    "First year", "Last year", "Recruits", "Deaths"))
```

Each row represents one individual at one annual census. Variables measured at
the beginning of the transition are labelled with `t0`, while measurements
from the following annual census are labelled with `t1`. A `t1` measurement is
only available when the individual has a valid transition to the next annual
census.

The final dataset includes height, crown diameter, stem number, flowering stem
number, stage, recruitment, survival, growth, and quadrat-level disturbance.
Plant volume was calculated as a cylindrical size index:

\[
\text{volume} =
\pi \left(\frac{\text{crown diameter}}{2}\right)^2
\times \text{height}.
\]

Log-transformed height and volume variables, including quadratic and cubic
terms, were added for later comparison of nonlinear vital-rate models.

```{r data-debugged-working-missingness}
df_work_missing <- tibble(
  variable = c(
    "survives", "size_t0", "size_t1",
    "volume_t0", "volume_t1", "dist_transition"),
  missing = c(
    sum(is.na(df_work$survives)),
    sum(is.na(df_work$size_t0)),
    sum(is.na(df_work$size_t1)),
    sum(is.na(df_work$volume_t0)),
    sum(is.na(df_work$volume_t1)),
    sum(is.na(df_work$dist_transition)))) %>%
  mutate(percent = 100 * missing / nrow(df_work))

knitr::kable(
  df_work_missing,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Variable", "Missing records", "Percent missing"))
```

Missing `size_t1` and `volume_t1` values mainly represent individuals without a
valid consecutive annual transition. Missing `volume_t0` values occur mainly
among recruits for which crown diameter was not measured. These recruits are
retained in the dataset because they still contribute to recruitment counts,
even when they cannot be used in volume-based vital-rate models.

Disturbance remains missing when no fire classification is recorded for a
quadrat during a known fire event. The available data do not establish why a
classification is missing. These observations were therefore retained as
unknown rather than being classified as undisturbed.

## Sampling inventory

The following figure shows the quadrat-year combinations represented in the
individual demographic data. Each point indicates that at least one individual
record occurs for that quadrat and year. The figure therefore shows the
temporal coverage of the individual-level dataset, including gaps in annual
records and the reduction in individual demographic monitoring after 2022.

```{r data-debugged-sampling-inventory, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
df_sampling_inventory <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(quad),
    !is.na(year)) %>%
  distinct(quad, year)

fig_sampling <- ggplot(
  df_sampling_inventory,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = quad)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = sort(
      unique(df_sampling_inventory$year))) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling inventory",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Quadrat") +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1))

fig_sampling
```

Because this figure is constructed from individual records in
`Demog_longform`, the absence of a point means that no individual demographic
record is available for that quadrat-year. It does not necessarily demonstrate
that the quadrat was not visited. This distinction is especially important
after 2022, when Level 2 quadrats continued to provide quadrat-level counts but
no longer contributed complete individual demographic records.


## Monitoring levels after 2022

Following the 2022 field season, monitoring was reduced in a subset of the
permanent quadrats. The variable `lvl3` identifies whether a quadrat continued
under Level 3 individual demographic monitoring or was monitored using the
reduced Level 2 protocol.

The two monitoring levels contain different types of information:

```{r data-debugged-monitoring-level-definition}
df_level_definition <- tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Level 2`, ~`Level 3`,
  "Observation unit",
  "Whole quadrat",
  "Individually marked plants",
  "Information recorded",
  paste(
    "Total plants, flowering stems and stems",
    "within the quadrat"),
  paste(
    "Survival, recruitment, stage, size and flowering",
    "of individual plants"),
  "Main worksheet",
  "`QuadLevel`",
  "`Demog_longform`",
  "Use in this project",
  "Population counts and monitoring effort",
  "Annual transitions and vital-rate models")

knitr::kable(df_level_definition)
```

Level 3 monitoring follows individual plants through time. It therefore
provides the information required to estimate individual survival, growth,
flowering and recruitment. These records are stored in `Demog_longform` and
form the basis of the annual working dataset.

Level 2 monitoring does not follow individual plants. Instead, the field team
records quadrat-level totals, including the number of plants, flowering stems
and stems. These observations are stored in `QuadLevel`. Level 2 quadrats
therefore remain part of the monitoring programme, but they cannot provide
individual annual transitions.

The distribution of quadrats between the two monitoring levels and the
availability of recent count data are shown below.

```{r data-debugged-monitoring-level-summary}
df_level_summary <- df_quad %>%
  mutate(
    monitoring_level = case_when(
      lvl3 == 0 ~ "Level 2",
      lvl3 == 1 ~ "Level 3",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown")) %>%
  group_by(monitoring_level) %>%
  summarise(
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    sites = n_distinct(patch),
    count_2023 = sum(!is.na(n2023)),
    count_2024 = sum(!is.na(n2024)),
    count_2025 = sum(!is.na(n2025)),
    .groups = "drop")

knitr::kable(
  df_level_summary,
  col.names = c(
    "Monitoring level", "Quadrats", "Sites",
    "Quadrats with 2023 counts",
    "Quadrats with 2024 counts",
    "Quadrats with 2025 counts"))
```

The following table shows which monitoring levels contributed individual
demographic records from 2023 onward.

```{r data-debugged-monitoring-level-demography}
df_level_demography <- df_demog_long %>%
  filter(year >= 2023) %>%
  dplyr::select(unique_id, quad, year) %>%
  left_join(
    df_quad %>%
      dplyr::select(quad, lvl3),
    by = "quad") %>%
  mutate(
    monitoring_level = case_when(
      lvl3 == 0 ~ "Level 2",
      lvl3 == 1 ~ "Level 3",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown")) %>%
  group_by(monitoring_level) %>%
  summarise(
    demographic_records = n(),
    individuals = n_distinct(unique_id),
    quadrats = n_distinct(quad),
    .groups = "drop")

knitr::kable(
  df_level_demography,
  col.names = c(
    "Monitoring level", "Demographic records",
    "Individuals", "Quadrats"))
```

This distinction is important when interpreting changes in the number of
records after 2022. A reduction in individual records does not necessarily
represent a decline in the population. It can also reflect the change from
Level 3 individual monitoring to Level 2 quadrat-level counts.

The working dataset is constructed from `Demog_longform` and therefore uses
individual-level observations. Level 2 data must be analysed separately or
explicitly incorporated as quadrat-level counts. Raw population totals from
the working dataset should consequently not be compared across the monitoring
change without accounting for the number and type of quadrats sampled.
